passage: Nilesh could ride only a few metres before his legs stopped and his feet dropped. Every day the same. "I'm not getting anywhere," he told Rajni, kicking the tyre. "Maybe you are," said Rajni. "You never measured." That evening Nilesh took chalk and drew a line at ten metres, another at twenty. The next day he reached the first line on his second try. The day after, he passed it easily and fell just before the second line. He rubbed his knee, but he was grinning, because he could now see that each attempt took him further than the last.

qa.q: What did Nilesh draw on the ground?
qa.a: Nilesh drew a line at ten metres and another at twenty.

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel when he told Rajni he was not getting anywhere?
qa.a: Nilesh felt stuck and discouraged, which is why he kicked the tyre.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nilesh try, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask an older rider to watch and point out one thing to fix. A fresh pair of eyes can spot problems that are hard to feel.

qa.q: How might Rajni see the chalk lines?
qa.a: Rajni might be pleased that the remark about never measuring turned into real marks on the ground that Nilesh now rides toward.

grounding: Feeling stuck at a few metres, a boy chalks ten- and twenty-metre marks so counting improvement shows him he is getting better despite falls.

passage:
"I'm stuck, Chandrika didi. I get three metres and fall. Every time."
"Every time? Let's check." She picked up a stick of chalk from the rangoli box. "Here's your start line. Here, ten big steps away, a line. That's ten metres, roughly."
"Ten? I can't do ten."
"Then fall and try again. I'll mark where you put your foot down."
Omkar rode. Fell. She drew a small cross. Rode again. Another cross, a little further.
"Didi, that one's past the last one!"
"And that one's past that."
By dinner, six crosses crept toward the line and one sat right on it.
"Tomorrow," Omkar said, "draw the twenty line."

qa.q: What did Chandrika use to mark where Omkar put his foot down?
qa.a: She used a stick of chalk from the rangoli box to draw a small cross.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he saw a cross past the last one?
qa.a: He felt excited and encouraged, because he could see he was getting further even though he still fell.

qa.q: What other approach could help Omkar after reaching twenty, and why?
qa.a: He could try riding a curve around a flowerpot, because a new small target keeps practice interesting once distance feels easy.

qa.q: How does the chalk plan look to Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika sees it as an easy way to show Omkar his progress, and she is probably glad to see his mood change.

grounding: It shows a boy who feels stuck at a few metres using chalk marks and ten- and twenty-metre goals to see his progress.

subtype: Approach: setting small goals such as ten metres, then twenty [Revision]
passage: For a whole week I thought I was hopeless at cycling. I'd ride a few metres, wobble and put a foot down. Always the same, I thought. Then on Saturday I took the chalk from my school bag and drew a line across our lane, ten metres from the gate. I said to myself, forget riding forever, just reach the line. First try, no. Fourth try, yes. So I drew another line, twenty metres. My sister Uma counted for me from the gate: "Yusuf, twelve! Fifteen! Eighteen!" I fell a lot. But every fall was further along, and I could see it on the road. On Monday I passed twenty. My knees are scraped, but I'm not hopeless any more.

qa.q: How far from the gate was the first chalk line?
qa.a: The first chalk line was ten metres from the gate.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel before drawing the chalk line?
qa.a: Yusuf felt hopeless and stuck, sure that every ride ended the same way.

qa.q: What would you change first if Yusuf got stuck again at twenty metres?
qa.a: Yusuf could draw smaller steps, such as every five metres, so progress is visible even on a hard day.

qa.q: How might the chalk lines look to Uma as she counts?
qa.a: Uma can hear and see progress in the numbers, so counting probably makes Uma feel part of Yusuf's success.

grounding: It shows a child who felt stuck at a few metres setting chalk goals of ten and then twenty metres and counting improvement.
